subject: ela
description: Students analyze an informational text to explain in detail how a key individual, event, or idea is introduced, illustrated, and elaborated across the text. They identify where and how the author first brings up the subject (introduction), trace the specific examples, anecdotes, facts, descriptions, or comparisons the author uses to illustrate it, and explain how the author develops, expands, or deepens it as the text moves forward (elaboration). They connect these moves, showing how each part builds on the one before to develop the reader's understanding of the person, event, or concept. Because this is a reading standard, every item embeds the full passage or excerpt it depends on, so the student needs nothing external to answer.
subSkills: Identify the key individual, event, or idea that an informational passage develops
Locate how and where the author introduces the subject and recognize the function of that introduction
Identify the specific means the author uses to illustrate the subject (examples, anecdotes, facts, statistics, descriptions, comparisons, or quotations)
Explain how the author elaborates on the subject across the text, building, expanding, or deepening it from one part to the next
Analyze how a particular detail or paragraph functions to introduce, illustrate, or elaborate the key subject
Trace the connection between parts of the text, showing how the development of the subject moves from introduction to fuller understanding

problemArchetypes.name: Identify how the subject is introduced
problemArchetypes.example: Read the short passage embedded in the item, then explain how the author first introduces the key individual, event, or idea: 'How does the author introduce the invention of the printing press in the first paragraph?' Answer names the way the introduction is made (a question, a striking fact, a brief story) and what it establishes for the reader.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the means of illustration
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage, then identify how the author illustrates the subject: 'Which example does the author use to show how harmful single-use plastic can be?' Answer points to the specific anecdote, fact, statistic, or description the author provides as evidence or illustration.

problemArchetypes.name: Explain how the subject is elaborated
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage, then explain how the author develops the idea across paragraphs: 'How does the second paragraph build on the first to deepen the reader's understanding of Harriet Tubman's courage?' Answer connects the two parts and names how the later part expands or deepens the earlier point.

problemArchetypes.name: Function of a specific detail or paragraph
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage, then determine the job a particular sentence or paragraph does: 'What is the main purpose of the third paragraph in the passage?' Answer states whether the part introduces, illustrates, or elaborates the key subject and explains how it serves that purpose.

problemArchetypes.name: Trace the development across the whole text
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage, then describe the overall path the author takes to develop the subject: 'Trace how the author develops the idea of the water cycle from the beginning of the passage to the end.' Answer follows the sequence from introduction through illustration to elaboration and shows how the parts connect.

problemArchetypes.name: Compare how two parts treat the subject
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage, then compare two moments in the text: 'How does the way the author talks about the volcano at the end differ from how it is introduced at the start?' Answer contrasts the introduction with a later elaboration and explains how the author's treatment has deepened or shifted.

Easy.description: A short, plainly written informational passage (roughly 80 to 130 words) that develops one clear subject in a straightforward order, embedded in the item. The task is to identify: where the subject is introduced, name one example the author gives to illustrate it, or state what a clearly marked detail does. The answer is stated or strongly signaled on the surface; little inference is required.
constraints: Stimulus is one short, single-topic informational passage (about 80 to 130 words) included in the prompt
The key individual, event, or idea is named explicitly and developed in plain chronological or list order
Identify-level task: find the introduction, name one illustrating example, or state what an obvious detail does
The introduction and illustrating details are stated explicitly; no multi-step inference needed

Medium.description: A moderately complex informational passage (roughly 150 to 250 words) that develops a subject across two or more connected paragraphs using more than one means of illustration, embedded in the item. The task requires analysis: explain how one part builds on another to elaborate the subject, identify the function of a paragraph, or explain how a chosen example supports the author's development of the idea. The answer is supported by the text but not stated word for word.
constraints: Stimulus is a multi-paragraph informational passage (about 150 to 250 words) included in the prompt
Tests how the subject is elaborated, the function of a paragraph, or how an illustration develops the idea
Analyze-level task: explain how or why parts connect to develop the subject, using evidence
Some inference required; the function of a detail or the link between parts is shown, not stated directly

Hard.description: A longer or more layered informational passage (roughly 280 to 420 words) that introduces a subject and develops it through several stages, using varied means of illustration and elaboration, embedded in the item. The task requires evaluation and synthesis: trace the full development of the subject from introduction to elaboration, judge which part best illustrates or most deepens the idea, or explain how the author's choices across multiple paragraphs combine to build the reader's understanding. Requires sustained inference across multiple parts of the text.
constraints: Stimulus is a longer informational passage (about 280 to 420 words) included in the prompt
Develops the subject in several stages with varied illustration and layered elaboration
Evaluate or synthesize task: trace the whole development, judge which part most illustrates or deepens the idea, or explain how parts combine
Requires inference that draws on evidence from several places in the passage

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses introducing a subject with elaborating on it, treating the first mention as if it already provides the full development
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an answer that calls the brief opening mention the author's full explanation, ignoring the later paragraphs that actually build out the idea

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student summarizes or retells the passage instead of explaining how the author introduces, illustrates, or elaborates the subject
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects an answer that restates what the passage says without naming the author's move (introduce, illustrate, or elaborate) or how the parts connect

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks a true detail from the text that is not actually the example the author uses to illustrate the key subject
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a fact that appears in the passage but does not serve to illustrate the individual, event, or idea the question asks about

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student mislabels the function of a paragraph, calling an illustrating example the introduction or treating elaboration as merely repetition
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Identifies a paragraph that gives an example as the introduction, or says a paragraph just repeats the point when it actually deepens or extends it

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats each paragraph as unconnected and fails to see how the author builds the subject from one part to the next
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses an answer that describes a single part in isolation and does not show how the later part builds on or develops the earlier one

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student names a means of illustration (anecdote, statistic, comparison) that the author does not actually use in the passage
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks a type of evidence or illustration that sounds plausible but does not appear in the embedded text

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student identifies how the subject is developed but attributes the development to the wrong part of the text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Names a real elaboration or illustration but points to the wrong paragraph or sentence as the place where the author makes that move
